note: Posts from TDI-owned voice accounts. Comments describe the tool, what to change, or who it suits. None claims a classroom moment.

posts: One line, and it has to be specific. Great week is a form letter and the family reads it as one.
Send the first batch to the families who usually only hear from school when something is wrong. That is where this earns the most.
Who would you send the first one to, and why that student?
Has a note home ever changed how a family dealt with you afterwards?
Designed for the first month, when you do not know them yet. It works later too but it is answering a different question by then.
Keep the reflection question the same for a week at a time. Changing it daily means you are comparing nothing to nothing.
What question do you ask that gets you a real answer rather than a shrug?
Does five minutes hold, or does it grow once students realise you are actually listening?
One to one, and the script opens without an accusation, because you almost never have proof of the thing you suspect.
Have the conversation somewhere the rest of the class cannot watch. Most of what goes wrong here is about the audience.
What do you do when the student denies it and you are fairly sure?
Does your department agree on what happens after this conversation?
Check who leads each organisation before you partner. Autistic-led and autism-adjacent are different things and families notice which one you brought in.
The partnership guide is more useful than the directory if you are starting from nothing.
Has your school partnered with an organisation for this? How did you choose?
What went wrong the first time you tried something like this?
Read the parent handouts before sending them. Families of autistic children have usually read a great deal already and can tell immediately whether you have.
The teacher guide assumes a mainstream classroom. If you are in a specialist setting, most of it will be behind where you are.
What would you want said to your class, if you were a parent of an autistic child in it?
How do you mark this month without making a single student the exhibit?
Decide your three sentences before the night rather than during it. Everything else on the checklist is logistics around those three.
The families you most want to meet are usually the ones who do not come. Worth planning what happens the next day for them.
What is the one thing you make sure to say to every family who walks in?
For leaders, what makes a good back-to-school night from the building's side rather than the classroom's?
The practical details are what families actually keep. The introduction is what they read once.
If you send this in more than one language, have a person check it. A machine translation of a welcome letter reads as exactly that.
What do you put in yours that is not in the template?
Paper, email, or both? I would expect the answer to differ a lot by building.
Concrete moves rather than a values poster, which is the right call. Respect on a wall changes nothing about how students speak to each other.
These work best introduced one at a time. All of them at once reads as a crackdown.
Which move here would your class find hardest?
What do you do about the student who is respectful to adults and not to peers?
Three audiences on one sheet, and the colleague section is the one people are least likely to have thought about.
Useful for anyone new to a building, where the problem is not what to say but who to say it to.
What is your reliable opener with a student who does not want to talk?
What works with a colleague you do not know well and have to work with closely?
Personalise one line at minimum. A message that is entirely template reads as one, and families compare notes.
The hardest scenarios here are the ones where you need to say something is not working. Those are worth rehearsing rather than sending cold.
Which parent message do you find hardest to write?
What have you added to your own copy-paste set that is not in here?
One page per check-in keeps a caseload readable. Longer notes feel more thorough and get read less.
The follow-up plan is the field that makes the log useful later. Reason and topics alone tell you what happened, not what you owe.
Who else sees these where you work, and does the student know that?
How do you decide what belongs in the log and what stays between you and the student?
The opening matters more than the rest. A call that starts badly cannot really be recovered inside the same call.
Sharing a concern without a verdict attached is the skill this is teaching. Most of us arrive with the verdict already formed.
What is your opening line on a call you are dreading?
Do you call, or do you write first and then call? I suspect that choice decides half of it.
Writing during the conference rather than after it is the point. Notes reconstructed an hour later quietly become your version of the meeting.
Tell the family you are taking notes and why. Silent writing across a table reads as something else entirely.
How do you take notes without losing eye contact for the whole meeting?
Do you share the agreed next steps back to the family afterwards?
Name one specific thing per student. Growth this year is what everyone writes and nobody remembers.
Worth writing in May rather than the last week, when you have more of the year in mind and less to do.
What do families say back to you about these, if anything?
How do you write one for a student whose year was genuinely hard?
The value of a log is entirely in it being complete. A log with the easy calls in it and not the hard ones is worse than none.
Log the attempt as well as the contact. Three unreturned calls is a record that matters later.
Has a log of yours ever been asked for? What was it needed for?
How do you keep this up in a week where everything is behind?
The same framework for students and colleagues is a stronger claim than it looks, and mostly it holds. The pacing is what changes.
Feedback that cannot be acted on this week is commentary. That is the filter worth applying to everything here.
What feedback have you been given that actually changed something you do?
Is giving feedback to a colleague harder than to a student, or just different?
Telling families the role is what stops a parent doing the whole project for the student who was assigned research.
Be explicit about what support looks like at home. Families guess, and they guess generously.
What does help at home actually mean for a group project in your subject?
How do you handle the group where one student did everything?
Parent-facing, so send it rather than summarising it. The anxiety this addresses is usually about the building and the timetable rather than the work.
Best sent in spring of the year before, not in September. By September the worry has already happened.
What do families ask you most about the move up?
What surprised you about middle school when you first taught it?
The visual supports carry most of the load at this age. The words are for the adults.
Works for any child who is not yet speaking much, not only for language learners. Worth knowing before you file it away.
What is your first move with a five year old who has no English and has just arrived?
How do you communicate with the family in that first week?
Shared is the important word. A log only one person writes in is a diary.
Built for people who are in four rooms a day and belong to none of them, which is a communication problem no classroom system solves.
How many rooms are you in during a day, and how do messages reach you now?
What gets lost most often between classrooms where you are?
Fast and fill-in, because a related-service provider finishing a pull-out has the next student waiting in the corridor.
The essentials here are what the classroom teacher needs, not what the report needs. Those are two different documents.
Does the classroom teacher get anything back after a pull-out where you work?
What would you want to know as the teacher receiving a student back?
A short form, handed over, rather than a conversation caught in a doorway. The doorway version is what this replaces and it loses things daily.
Write the small stuff. The teacher already knows about the big incident, and it is the quiet detail from second period that turns out to matter.
How does your handover happen now, and does anything reliably get through?
For teachers, what do you most want to know from the person who was with your students while you were not?
Coach-facing, and the deliverable is language the teacher can actually say out loud. A prep session that ends in strategy and no sentences has not worked.
Twenty minutes before a hard conference is worth more than an hour afterwards, and it is much harder to schedule.
For coaches, how do you prepare a teacher who is defensive about the conference itself?
Has anyone ever prepped you before a hard conference? What did they do?
